title: Contending for the Faith Once Delivered
summary: Jude warns against intruders who twist grace into license and calls the beloved to contend, persevere, rescue others, and trust God’s keeping power.
historicalContext: Jude writes as the brother of James and therefore, most naturally, as one of the Lord’s brothers who came to faith after the resurrection. The letter names no city, yet its readers plainly knew the Hebrew Scriptures well and also the stories that Jewish teachers had built around them, such as the dispute over Moses’ body and the prophecy of Enoch. Itinerant teachers had entered their fellowship and shared their love feasts. These men claimed visionary insight, treated God’s grace as permission for sexual and moral license, despised authority, and drew followers after themselves for profit. Much of Jude’s material reappears in 2 Peter 2, which shows that the same threat troubled more than one congregation in the apostolic generation. Jude’s brief, urgent letter belongs to a church that had received the apostles’ teaching and now had to decide whether that teaching would govern its life.
literaryContext: The letter is short but built with great care. A greeting (vv. 1–2) and a doxology (vv. 24–25) frame it with God’s keeping power, so that every warning stands inside a promise. Verses 3–4 state the purpose: contend for the faith because ungodly men have slipped in. The long central section (vv. 5–19) sets ancient examples beside present application, often joined by the pointer “these.” Israel in the wilderness, the rebel angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah, Enoch’s prophecy, and the apostles’ prediction each expose the intruders and announce their end. Jude loves groups of three and vivid imagery drawn from sky, earth, sea, and stars. The closing exhortation (vv. 20–23) turns from the false teachers to the faithful, showing what contending looks like in practice: building, praying, keeping, waiting, and rescuing those in danger.
themes: The faith once for all delivered to the saints
Grace that produces holiness rather than license
God’s certain judgment on persistent rebellion
The great controversy behind earthly conflict
Persevering in God’s love while awaiting Christ’s mercy
God’s power to keep His people from falling

outline.title: Greeting to the Called and Kept
outline.summary: Jude addresses believers loved by the Father and kept for Jesus Christ, praying that mercy, peace, and love abound.

outline.title: The Urgent Call to Contend
outline.summary: News of intruders who pervert grace and deny Christ compels Jude to urge a vigorous defense of the apostolic faith.

outline.title: Ancient Patterns and Present Intruders
outline.summary: Examples from Israel, angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah, and Enoch expose the false teachers and announce their certain judgment.

outline.title: Remembering, Persevering, and Rescuing
outline.summary: Recalling the apostles’ warning, the faithful build on their holy faith, keep in God’s love, and reach out to those in danger.

outline.title: Praise to the God Who Keeps
outline.summary: Jude closes by giving eternal glory to the only God, who can keep His people and present them faultless with joy.

verses.bibleText: Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Jude” is the English form of Judas, the Greek spelling of the honored tribal name Judah. Among several men of that name in the New Testament, the writer identifies himself by his brother. The James who needed no further description in the early church was the leader of the Jerusalem believers, the brother of the Lord (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19). The Gospels list a Judas among the brothers of Jesus (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3), so the writer is almost certainly that man. During Jesus’ ministry His brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:5). After the resurrection they are found praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14).

What Jude leaves unsaid is telling. He could have opened with his family tie to Jesus. Instead he calls himself “the servant of Jesus Christ,” a bondservant who belongs to a Master. The one who grew up in the same home now bows before Him as Lord. Such reticence carries its own authority: Jude speaks as one under orders, and that is the only standing he claims.

The readers are described before they are warned. The earliest manuscripts read “beloved in God the Father” where the KJV has “sanctified,” yet either reading fixes attention on what God has done. They are loved or set apart by the Father, “preserved in Jesus Christ,” and “called.” Each description places the initiative with God. The calling came from Him, the love rests on them from Him, and the keeping is His work.

This opening prepares for everything that follows. Jude is about to describe intruders, apostasy, and judgment in the sharpest language of the New Testament. Before a single warning is given, he assures the faithful that they are held. The word “preserved” will return in the command “keep yourselves in the love of God” (v. 21) and in the closing praise to Him “that is able to keep you from falling” (v. 24).

wordNotes.explanation: The perfect participle describes people who have been kept and remain under guard. The phrase may mean kept by Christ or kept for Christ until His coming, and both ideas fit Jude’s purpose. The same verb family reappears in the letter, both for the faithful who must keep themselves (v. 21) and for the rebels reserved for judgment (vv. 6, 13).

Jude places this word last for emphasis. In the New Testament it describes those who have heard and answered God’s summons in the gospel; it is a name for believers. Their identity begins with God’s call rather than with their own achievement.

verses.bibleText: Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Christian letters usually opened with a prayer for grace and peace. Jude offers a triad of his own: “Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied.” Mercy is God’s compassion toward those who deserve nothing and need everything. Peace is the wholeness and reconciliation that follow when that mercy is received. Love names the Father’s steady, unchanging affection already mentioned in verse 1, now extended and enlarged in their experience.

The absence of “grace” may be deliberate. The intruders were turning “the grace of our God into lasciviousness” (v. 4), and Jude may have chosen words that could not be twisted in the same way. Whatever the reason, the three blessings he names return at the letter’s end. The readers are to keep themselves “in the love of God,” look for “the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 21), and show mercy to the wavering (vv. 22–23). The greeting therefore announces what the letter hopes to accomplish. Jude wants these gifts increased, multiplied beyond their present measure, in a church under pressure, because a congregation rich in mercy, peace, and love is far harder for error to divide.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb is in the optative mood, the form used for a wish or prayer. Jude asks God to increase these blessings, as a seed increases into a harvest. The same greeting formula appears in Peter’s letters and echoes the royal greeting of Daniel.

verses.bibleText: Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jude lets his readers see the letter he intended to write. He was giving “all diligence” to a message about “the common salvation,” the salvation that every believer shares with every other, Jew and Gentile, leader and member alike. That would have been a positive letter of encouragement. Then a necessity pressed upon him. The expression “it was needful for me” suggests a sudden compulsion, a change of plan forced by news of what was happening among them. Under the Spirit’s guidance the planned treatise gave way to an urgent appeal.

The appeal is to “earnestly contend for the faith.” The verb belongs to the language of the athletic contest and the battlefield, and the prefix intensifies it. Jude calls for sustained, strenuous effort. Every member is addressed. He does not ask them to watch while their leaders defend the truth; he exhorts them all to take up the struggle.

What they defend is “the faith,” with the article: the body of truth about Christ and the life He requires, as the apostles proclaimed it. Personal trust is included, yet the emphasis falls on the content believed. This faith “was once delivered unto the saints.” The word “once” means once for all. God handed this truth to His people through Christ and His apostles in a decisive act, and it does not need supplementing by later revelations that contradict it. The intruders claimed visions (v. 8); Jude measures every such claim by what had already been delivered.

The word “delivered” describes a sacred trust passed from hand to hand. The church does not invent its message; it receives, guards, and transmits what has been given. “The saints” are the whole company of believers, set apart for God. Contending, as the close of the letter will show, includes building one another up, praying, keeping in God’s love, and rescuing those drawn into error (vv. 20–23). Contention of this sort is fidelity under pressure, carried out in love, and it leaves no room for a merely combative temperament.

wordNotes.explanation: Found only here in the New Testament, this strengthened verb pictures an athlete straining in competition or a soldier in combat. The present tense calls for ongoing effort. Paul uses the simpler related verb for the believer’s fight of faith, and Jesus for striving to enter the narrow gate.

Hapax means once for all, describing something completed and unrepeatable, as with Christ’s sacrifice. The participle comes from the verb used for handing on authoritative teaching. Together they describe the apostolic gospel as a finished deposit entrusted to the church, the standard by which every later claim must be tested.

verses.bibleText: For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here is the reason for Jude’s urgency: “there are certain men crept in unawares.” The verb pictures someone slipping in through a side entrance. These men did not announce themselves as enemies of the gospel. They came as teachers and fellow believers, sat at the church’s love feasts (v. 12), and worked from within. Their presence was the more dangerous because it was unsuspected.

They were “before of old ordained to this condemnation.” The Greek speaks of being written about beforehand. Jude is describing a judgment already on record against such conduct; he is not teaching that God decreed certain individuals to sin and be lost. The ancient examples that follow (vv. 5–7, 11) and the prophecy of Enoch (vv. 14–15) are that record. Scripture had long ago described the end of those who rebel against God, and these men had placed themselves within that description.

Jude gives three charges. They are “ungodly men,” a word that will ring through the letter, culminating in the fourfold “ungodly” of verse 15. They lack reverence for God. Next, they were “turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness.” They took the free pardon of the gospel and made it an excuse for unrestrained sensuality, reasoning perhaps that those under grace were no longer bound by moral law. Paul had met the same error and answered it plainly: shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid (Romans 6:1–2). The grace that brings salvation teaches us to deny ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). It pardons the transgressor of God’s law and then writes that law on the heart.

Finally, they were “denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.” The oldest manuscripts lack “God,” so the phrase may be read as one title: our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. The word for “Lord” in the first phrase means a sovereign owner. These men may have confessed Christ with their lips, yet they refused to live under His rule. In conduct they denied the One who bought them.

The verse warns that the deepest threats to faith often come in familiar dress. Jude asks the church to judge teaching by its fruit and to recognize that any message making sin comfortable has abandoned the grace it claims to preach.

wordNotes.explanation: This verb, used only here in the New Testament, means to slip in secretly or worm one’s way in. Related words describe false brethren brought in privately and false teachers who introduce heresies stealthily. The image is of infiltration by people who look like insiders.

The word describes shameless, unrestrained indulgence, especially sexual excess, practiced without regard for decency or for the judgment of others. It appears in lists of the works of the flesh. Jude charges the intruders with presenting this conduct as the freedom that grace allows.

verses.bibleText: I will therefore put you in remembrance, though ye once knew this, how that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jude begins his evidence with history his readers already knew. “I will therefore put you in remembrance, though ye once knew this.” He is not teaching them something new; he is calling up what they had learned when they first received the faith. Forgetfulness, more than ignorance, is the danger. People who know the story of God’s dealings can still fail to apply it to themselves.

The first example is Israel in the wilderness. “The Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not.” Several early manuscripts read “Jesus” here in place of “the Lord,” a reading that agrees with Paul’s statement that the Rock which followed Israel was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). The One who redeemed Israel at the Red Sea was the same divine Lord now confessed as Jesus Christ. The deliverance was real. Israel ate the Passover, crossed the sea, and sang the song of Moses. Yet “afterward,” literally “the second time,” the same Lord acted in judgment. At Kadesh the people refused to enter the land, and that generation died in the desert (Numbers 14:26–35).

The force of the example lies in its starting point. These were redeemed people. Their failure was unbelief, a refusal to trust God’s word that showed itself in grumbling, rebellion, and disobedience. Jude’s readers had also been delivered, and the intruders among them claimed the privileges of grace. Hebrews draws the same lesson: they could not enter in because of unbelief (Hebrews 3:19). A past experience of salvation gives no immunity to those who later turn from the Saviour in persistent unbelief. The way to remain safe is to keep trusting the One who saved.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the second time.” The first act of the Lord was deliverance from Egypt; the second was judgment on those who refused to believe. The phrase sets the two acts side by side, showing that the God who saves is also the God who judges persistent unbelief.

wordNotes.term: μὴ πιστεύσαντας (mē pisteusantas) — them that believed not
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes people marked by refusal to trust God’s promise. In the wilderness accounts unbelief and disobedience are two sides of one failure: those who did not believe also did not obey.

verses.bibleText: And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second example moves from earth to heaven. Even angels, the highest of created beings, were not exempt from judgment when they rebelled. They “kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation.” The word rendered “first estate” means their original position, the sphere of rule and service God had assigned them. They abandoned it by choice.

Jewish writers of Jude’s day often connected this fall with the “sons of God” of Genesis 6. Jude does not develop that story. The wider testimony of Scripture places the angels’ rebellion in heaven itself, where Lucifer exalted himself against God and drew a host of angels after him (Isaiah 14:12–15; Revelation 12:7–9). Their sin was a revolt against God’s government, the first act in the great controversy between Christ and Satan that still shapes human history.

Jude makes a pointed play on words. The angels did not keep their place, so God “hath reserved,” or kept, them. Those who refused His keeping are now kept for judgment. “Everlasting chains under darkness” describes a restraint they cannot escape. Since Scripture also shows Satan and his angels active in the world (Ephesians 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8), the chains are best read as a figure for their confinement within limits God has set and for the moral darkness to which they have consigned themselves. They have no way back to the light they left.

Their final sentence still lies ahead: they are held “unto the judgment of the great day.” Jude does not picture them as already undergoing their ultimate punishment. They await the day when God will judge all rebellion, a day prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). If God did not spare angels who rejected His authority, no teacher who despises it can expect to escape.

wordNotes.explanation: The word often means “beginning,” yet it also denotes rule or domain, as in Paul’s references to principalities. Here it describes the original position of authority and service God assigned the angels. They did not guard what had been entrusted to them.

wordNotes.term: δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον (desmois aidiois hypo zophon) — everlasting chains under darkness
wordNotes.explanation: The bonds are “everlasting” in that the fallen angels can never break free from the condition into which their rebellion has placed them. The word for darkness suggests deep gloom. Peter uses similar language when he says they are delivered into chains of darkness and reserved unto judgment.

verses.bibleText: Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third example is the most visible. “Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them,” Admah and Zeboim (Deuteronomy 29:23), were overthrown in a single day. Jude says they acted “in like manner” to the angels just described. Both crossed boundaries God had set. The angels left their proper sphere; the men of Sodom pursued relations outside the order God established at creation.

They were “giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh.” The first expression is an intensive word describing complete abandonment to sexual immorality. “Strange flesh,” literally “other flesh,” recalls the men of the city who surrounded Lot’s house demanding to know his guests (Genesis 19:4–5). Ezekiel adds that Sodom’s guilt included pride, excess, idleness, and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50). Jude draws attention to the sexual corruption because the intruders of verse 4 were turning grace into lasciviousness.

These cities “are set forth for an example.” The word means to lie exposed to view. For centuries travelers could see the desolate region by the Dead Sea, a landscape that bore silent witness to what sin finally produces. God’s judgment there was public so that later generations might take warning (2 Peter 2:6).

They are described as “suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.” The fire that fell on Sodom is called eternal, yet Sodom is not burning today. That fire did its work completely: it reduced the cities to ashes (2 Peter 2:6), and when nothing remained to consume, it went out. Its result has never been reversed; the cities were never rebuilt and never will be. “Eternal” here describes a fire whose effect is permanent, a judgment that belongs to the age to come in its finality. The punishment they continue to bear is their state of utter destruction.

This gives an important key for reading other passages about the fate of the lost. Jude offers Sodom as a pattern of final judgment, and the pattern is destruction that cannot be undone. The example gives no support to the idea of unending conscious torment. The wicked will be consumed, “burned up” so that neither root nor branch remains (Malachi 4:1), suffering “everlasting destruction” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). Even in this warning God’s mercy appears, for before the fire fell, angels led Lot and his daughters out of the city.

wordNotes.explanation: The adjective aiōnios often describes what belongs to the coming age and therefore what is final and lasting. Sodom’s fire is called eternal because its result is permanent, although the flames themselves ended long ago. Jeremiah likewise speaks of an unquenchable fire that would devour Jerusalem’s palaces; it burned until its work was done and could not be stopped.

Literally “other” or “different flesh.” The phrase describes sexual pursuit outside the boundaries of the creation order, as the men of Sodom sought relations with Lot’s male visitors. Jude sets it parallel to the angels who left their proper habitation.

verses.bibleText: Likewise also these filthy dreamers defile the flesh, despise dominion, and speak evil of dignities.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Likewise also these.” With that pointer Jude turns from the ancient examples to the intruders. Despite the warning written over Israel, the angels, and Sodom, they repeat the same pattern. The word “filthy” was supplied by the KJV translators from the context. Jude calls them simply “dreamers,” which most likely refers to their claims of visionary experience. They justified their conduct by appeal to revelations, dreams that gave them insight others supposedly lacked. Such claims set private experience above the faith once delivered (v. 3). Scripture had long warned against prophets who dream dreams to lead God’s people away from His commandments (Deuteronomy 13:1–5).

Three charges follow, each echoing the examples just given. They “defile the flesh,” like Sodom. They “despise dominion,” refusing the lordship of Christ much as Israel rejected the Lord’s leading in the wilderness. And they “speak evil of dignities,” literally “glories,” probably meaning glorious angelic beings. Perhaps they mocked the angels as guardians of the moral order they wished to escape, or ridiculed spiritual powers they did not understand.

The common thread is contempt for authority. Moral impurity, rebellion against Christ’s rule, and scorn for heavenly realities belong together. When people decide that their own visions outrank God’s word, every boundary becomes negotiable.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to have dreams or visions. The same verb appears in Joel’s promise that old men shall dream dreams, yet it is also used of false prophets whose dreams lead people away from God. Jude implies that the intruders based their authority on such revelations.
Literally “glories.” In this context the word most likely refers to angelic beings who share in God’s glory. The verse that follows, with its picture of Michael and the devil, supports this reading.

verses.bibleText: Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Against the intruders’ contempt for heavenly beings Jude sets a striking scene: “Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.”

The identity of Michael deserves careful attention. His name asks a question, “Who is like God?” In Daniel he is “the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people,” the One who rises at the time of the end when the dead are awakened (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1–2). In Revelation, Michael and His angels make war on the dragon and cast him out of heaven (Revelation 12:7–9). Paul says the Lord descends “with the voice of the archangel” to raise the dead (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and Jesus said the dead will hear His own voice and come forth (John 5:28–29). Taken together, these passages point to Michael as a name of Christ Himself. “Archangel” then means chief or ruler of the angels, the Commander of heaven’s armies; it does not place Him among created angels. Christ is the Creator of the angels (Colossians 1:16), and they are commanded to worship Him (Hebrews 1:6).

The dispute concerned Moses’ body. Deuteronomy records that Moses died on Mount Nebo and that the Lord buried him in a place no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:5–6). Centuries later Moses appeared with Elijah on the mount of transfiguration (Matthew 17:3; Luke 9:30–31). Elijah had been taken to heaven without dying; Moses had died. His presence there implies that he had been raised from the grave. The contest Jude describes is best understood as Satan’s resistance to that resurrection. The accuser could point to Moses’ sin at Meribah (Numbers 20:10–12) and claim the body as his lawful prey. Christ prevailed, and Moses became a pledge of the resurrection that awaits all who sleep in Jesus. Jude appears to draw the account from a Jewish tradition about Moses’ death; citing a true incident from such a source does not make the whole writing inspired.

The point of the illustration is Michael’s restraint. Even facing the devil, He would not pronounce a slanderous verdict. Accusation is Satan’s weapon (Revelation 12:10), and Christ refused to fight with it. He committed the matter to the Father’s judgment in words that echo Zechariah 3:2, where the Lord rebukes Satan for accusing Joshua the high priest.

The intruders “speak evil of dignities” (v. 8) with a boldness the Lord of the angels never used. The faithful are taught to speak about evil with seriousness and without scorn, leaving final condemnation to God.

wordNotes.term: Μιχαὴλ ὁ ἀρχάγγελος (Michaēl ho archangelos) — Michael the archangel
wordNotes.explanation: The title combines the prefix for “chief” or “ruler” with the word for “messenger.” It appears in the New Testament only here and in Paul’s description of the Lord’s descent, when the voice of the archangel raises the dead. Read with Daniel’s portrait of Michael as the great prince who stands for God’s people, it describes the One who leads heaven’s hosts and who calls the dead from their graves.

wordNotes.term: Ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι κύριος (Epitimēsai soi kyrios) — The Lord rebuke thee
wordNotes.explanation: The words repeat Zechariah’s vision, in which Satan stands to accuse the high priest Joshua and the Lord answers by rebuking the accuser. The optative expresses an appeal: the verdict is left with God. Jesus later rebuked demons, winds, and even Peter with the same verb.

verses.bibleText: But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But these speak evil of those things which they know not.” The intruders boasted of special insight, yet Jude says they are ignorant of the very realm they mock. The heavenly order of glory, angels, and divine authority lies beyond their understanding, and so they treat it with contempt. Ignorance that refuses correction becomes arrogance.

There is something they do understand: “what they know naturally, as brute beasts.” Their knowledge is the knowledge of instinct and appetite, the kind animals possess without reflection. They know how to satisfy hunger and desire. That knowledge, followed without restraint, becomes the means of their ruin: “in those things they corrupt themselves.” The verb can mean both to be morally corrupted and to be destroyed. The appetites they indulge are destroying them. Self-proclaimed visionaries are exposed as people governed by impulse, and the path they call freedom leads to their undoing (Galatians 6:7–8).

wordNotes.explanation: The adverb describes knowledge by natural instinct, apart from reason or revelation. Jude pairs it with “brute beasts,” literally creatures without reason, to show that the intruders live at the level of appetite while claiming spiritual insight.

The verb means to ruin, spoil, or destroy. It can describe moral decay or final destruction, and here both ideas meet. Paul warns that whoever defiles the temple of God, God will destroy, using the same verb.

verses.bibleText: Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Woe unto them!” Jude speaks with a prophet’s voice. The woe is both a cry of grief and a pronouncement of judgment, the form Jesus used against the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23:13–36). Three Old Testament figures follow, each one exposing a further side of the intruders’ character.

They “have gone in the way of Cain.” Cain approached God on his own terms, offering what he chose and refusing the offering God had appointed (Genesis 4:3–7; Hebrews 11:4). When his worship was not accepted, envy hardened into hatred and hatred into murder. John says Cain “was of that wicked one” (1 John 3:12). Jewish teachers came to regard Cain as the pattern of the cynic who despises God’s justice and leads others to do the same. The intruders follow this road of self-chosen religion, and by drawing others into sin they become destroyers of souls.

They “ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward.” The verb pictures water poured out, an abandonment to a course of action. Balaam knew the true God, yet he loved the wages of unrighteousness (2 Peter 2:15). Unable to curse Israel, he counseled Balak to seduce them into immorality and idolatry at Baal-peor, and twenty-four thousand died (Numbers 25:1–9; 31:16). The intruders, like Balaam, used religious gifts for profit and led God’s people into sexual sin.

They “perished in the gainsaying of Core.” Korah, with Dathan and Abiram, rose against the authority God had given Moses and Aaron, claiming that all the congregation was equally holy and needed no appointed leaders (Numbers 16:1–3). The earth opened and swallowed the rebels, and fire consumed the two hundred and fifty who offered incense (Numbers 16:31–35). Jude writes “perished” in the past tense, as though the intruders’ end had already happened. Their rebellion has placed them on Korah’s ground, and the outcome is as certain as his.

The progression is sobering: a way taken, an error embraced, a destruction sealed.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to pour out, as wine or blood is poured. In the passive it describes people who have abandoned themselves to something, flowing after it without restraint. Here it pictures eager, reckless surrender to Balaam’s greed.

The word means contradiction or speaking against, and so rebellion. The Greek Old Testament uses related language for the waters of Meribah, the place of strife. Hebrews uses the term for the hostility sinners directed against Christ.

verses.bibleText: These are spots in your feasts of charity, when they feast with you, feeding themselves without fear: clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jude now piles up images, beginning at the church’s own table. “These are spots in your feasts of charity.” The word translated “spots” most likely means hidden reefs, rocks just beneath the surface that tear open the hulls of ships. The intruders were present at the love feasts, the fellowship meals at which believers ate together and shared the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:20–22). Their presence there made them more dangerous; what looked like fellowship was a hazard waiting to wreck the faith of others.

They feast “without fear,” brazenly and without reverence, and “feeding themselves.” The verb means to shepherd. Ezekiel rebuked the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves instead of the flock (Ezekiel 34:2, 8). These men had assumed a leading place in the congregation and used it to serve their own appetites.

The next two images come from sky and orchard. They are “clouds without water, carried about of winds.” In a dry land, gathering clouds raise hope of rain, and Proverbs compares a man who boasts of a false gift to clouds and wind without rain (Proverbs 25:14). The intruders promised spiritual refreshment and delivered nothing; they were driven by every wind of their own desires. They are “trees whose fruit withereth,” better rendered “autumn trees,” barren at the very season when fruit is expected. Jesus taught that a tree is known by its fruit (Matthew 7:17–20).

Such trees are “twice dead, plucked up by the roots.” They are dead in their fruitlessness and dead again because they have been torn from the soil. The phrase may also recall that these men, once dead in sin, had been brought near to life and then returned to death. Jesus warned that every plant His Father had not planted would be rooted up (Matthew 15:13). Uprooting is final; no life can return to such a tree.

wordNotes.explanation: In ordinary Greek usage the word described rocks hidden in the sea, a danger to sailors. A related word means stain or blemish, and Peter speaks of spots and blemishes in a parallel passage. Either sense fits: the intruders both defiled the fellowship and threatened to wreck it.

The plural of agapē, love, here names the shared meals of the early church, where believers ate together as a family and often celebrated the Lord’s Supper. The name itself expressed the love that was supposed to bind them, which made selfish behavior at these meals especially offensive.

verses.bibleText: Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The images move to the sea and the heavens. The intruders are “raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame.” Isaiah had described the wicked as a troubled sea that cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt (Isaiah 57:20). Wild waves throw scum and debris onto the beach. So these men put their shameful deeds on display, restless and uncontrolled, with no sense that such conduct ought to embarrass them.

They are also “wandering stars.” Travelers and sailors relied on the fixed stars for direction. A star that wanders, whether a planet moving irregularly or a meteor flaring across the sky, cannot guide anyone. The intruders might shine brightly for a moment, yet anyone who steers by them will be lost. Jewish tradition sometimes pictured fallen angels as stars that left their courses, which links this image to the rebel angels of verse 6.

For such stars “is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.” A meteor that plunges into the dark does not return. The picture is of a light extinguished permanently, a final separation from the God who is light. The phrase describes an irreversible sentence; it is no portrait of endless existence in pain. Scripture elsewhere says the wicked shall be as though they had not been (Obadiah 1:16) and shall consume away like smoke (Psalm 37:20).

wordNotes.explanation: The second word, from which English takes “planet,” comes from the verb meaning to wander or lead astray. Jude chooses an image that fits both the instability of the intruders and their effect on others: they wander and they cause others to wander.

wordNotes.term: ζόφος τοῦ σκότους (zophos tou skotous) — blackness of darkness
wordNotes.explanation: The doubled expression intensifies the idea of gloom: darkness at its deepest. The same phrase occurs in Peter’s parallel. It stands in contrast with the presence of God’s glory, which the faithful will enter with exceeding joy.

verses.bibleText: And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jude’s next witness reaches back before the flood. “Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these.” Counting in the ancient way, which includes both ends of the line, Enoch is seventh: Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch (Genesis 5:3–18). The detail may carry a quiet contrast. The seventh in Cain’s line was Lamech, who boasted of his violence (Genesis 4:19–24); the seventh in Seth’s line walked with God and was taken to heaven without seeing death (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5). The man who lived in closest fellowship with God in a corrupt age was given a message about its end.

The words Jude cites closely match a passage in the Jewish writing now called 1 Enoch, which circulated widely before the time of Christ. Jude calls the saying a prophecy and applies it to the intruders. Quoting a true statement from that tradition does not make the whole book of 1 Enoch Scripture, any more than Paul’s quotations of Greek poets give their works canonical standing (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Under the Spirit’s guidance Jude affirms that this particular word was true and that it described the people troubling the church.

The prophecy opens with a cry: “Behold, the Lord cometh.” The Greek verb is past tense, literally “came,” a prophetic way of speaking about a future event so certain that it can be described as already done. The Lord comes “with ten thousands of his saints,” literally “in His holy myriads.” These holy ones are the angelic hosts who attend Christ at His return (Deuteronomy 33:2; Zechariah 14:5; Matthew 25:31).

This may be the earliest recorded prophecy of the Second Coming. From the seventh generation of humanity, God’s people have looked for a personal, visible return of the Lord in glory to set right what sin has ruined. The intruders mocked that hope (v. 18), and Jude answers with a prophecy older than the flood.

wordNotes.term: ἦλθεν κύριος (ēlthen kyrios) — the Lord cometh
wordNotes.explanation: The aorist verb literally reads “the Lord came.” Hebrew prophecy often uses such a past tense for future events to stress their certainty, as when Isaiah speaks of the Child already born. The coming of the Lord is spoken of as settled fact.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν αὐτοῦ (en hagiais myriasin autou) — with ten thousands of his saints
wordNotes.explanation: A myriad is ten thousand, and the plural denotes a countless host. “Holy ones” in this setting most naturally refers to angels, who in Daniel’s vision stand by the ten thousand times ten thousand before the throne and who accompany the Son of man when He comes in His glory.

verses.bibleText: To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The prophecy states the purpose of the Lord’s coming: “to execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly.” Judgment comes to all, for every life will be reviewed before God. “Convince” here means to convict, to expose and prove guilty beyond dispute. On that day the ungodly will see their own deeds in the light of God’s justice and will have no defense.

Jude’s citation repeats the word “ungodly” four times: “all that are ungodly,” “their ungodly deeds,” deeds “which they have ungodly committed,” and words spoken by “ungodly sinners.” The repetition picks up Jude’s description of the intruders in verse 4 and fixes their character beyond question. Ungodliness, the refusal to reverence God, has worked its way into every part of their conduct.

The judgment covers words as well as acts: “all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.” Jesus taught that by our words we shall be justified or condemned (Matthew 12:36–37). The harsh, defiant things people say against God, often to excuse their own sin or to question His fairness, will be answered. This prepares for verse 16, where Jude lists the intruders’ sins of speech.

The final judgment also settles a larger question. Satan has accused God of injustice since the rebellion began. When the Lord comes, His ways will be shown to be true and righteous before the whole universe (Revelation 15:3–4).

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to expose, refute, or convict. Jesus promised that the Spirit would convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment. At the Lord’s coming that conviction becomes final and public, leaving the ungodly without excuse.
Literally “hard things,” meaning harsh, defiant words. The disciples once called Jesus’ teaching a hard saying. Here the hardness belongs to those who speak against God.

verses.bibleText: These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words, having men's persons in admiration because of advantage.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are murmurers, complainers.” Jude returns to the intruders and shows that Enoch’s description fits them. Murmuring was the characteristic sin of Israel in the wilderness, a low, sullen grumbling against Moses and finally against God (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27). The word itself imitates the sound of discontented muttering. “Complainers” are those who find fault with their lot, blaming God for the portion He has given them. Both terms reveal a heart at odds with God’s providence.

They are “walking after their own lusts.” Desire, not God’s will, sets their direction. Their speech matches their walk: “their mouth speaketh great swelling words,” arrogant, inflated claims about themselves and their supposed insight. Daniel saw a power with a mouth speaking great things against the Most High (Daniel 7:8; 11:36). Such boasting is the opposite of Michael’s restraint in verse 9.

Finally, they are “having men’s persons in admiration because of advantage.” They flatter people who can benefit them. James condemns this kind of partiality as a breach of the royal law (James 2:1–9). Grumbling toward God, boasting about self, flattering others for gain: the triad exposes speech that has lost its reverence. Paul’s counsel stands as the remedy: do all things without murmurings (Philippians 2:14).

wordNotes.explanation: The noun comes from a verb whose sound imitates grumbling under one’s breath. In the Greek Old Testament the related verb describes Israel’s complaints in the wilderness, and Paul warns the church not to murmur as some of them did.
The word describes something swollen beyond its proper size, and so speech that is inflated, pompous, and arrogant. Peter uses it for false teachers whose boastful words allure the unstable.

verses.bibleText: But, beloved, remember ye the words which were spoken before of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But, beloved.” The Greek places “ye” first for emphasis: as for you. Jude turns from the intruders to the faithful and calls them once more by the name of affection he used in verse 3.

His first instruction is to remember: “remember ye the words which were spoken before of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Jude speaks of the apostles as a group distinct from himself, consistent with his description of himself as a servant (v. 1). The apostles had warned the churches repeatedly that false teachers would arise from within (Acts 20:29–30; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1–5). Their warnings were part of the faith once delivered. Their words now stand written in the New Testament, still available to every congregation. Memory is one of the church’s defenses. When believers recall what Christ’s messengers foretold, the appearance of error confirms the reliability of the word instead of shaking their faith.

wordNotes.explanation: The imperative calls for active recollection that shapes present conduct. Biblical remembering goes beyond recalling information; it means letting what God has said govern how one responds now. Jesus urged His followers to remember His words about coming persecution.

verses.bibleText: How that they told you there should be mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jude summarizes the apostolic warning: “there should be mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts.” The same prediction appears almost word for word in 2 Peter 3:3, where the scoffers ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?”

“The last time” describes the whole period that began with Christ’s first coming and runs until His return. John could write that it was already the last hour because many antichrists had appeared (1 John 2:18). Every generation of believers lives in these last days, and each must be ready for mockery of the faith.

Jude traces the mocking to its source. The scoffers walk “after their own ungodly lusts,” literally “according to their own desires for ungodliness.” Ridicule of God’s promises and judgment often arises less from intellectual difficulty than from a wish to live without accountability. When the coming of the Lord is laughed away, so is the judgment that would call their conduct to account.

wordNotes.explanation: The word describes scoffers who treat serious things as a joke. The related verb is used of those who mocked Jesus at His trial and crucifixion. Jude and Peter alone use the noun in the New Testament.

wordNotes.term: ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτου χρόνου (ep’ eschatou chronou) — in the last time
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase names the final era of history inaugurated by Christ. Hebrews says God has spoken in these last days by His Son. The expression calls for watchfulness without setting dates.

verses.bibleText: These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jude adds his final description of the intruders: “These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit.” The verb behind “separate themselves” means to make distinctions or draw boundaries, and so to cause divisions. These men created factions in the church, perhaps by sorting believers into the spiritually advanced and the ordinary, with themselves in the first rank.

Jude overturns their claim. They are “sensual,” a word meaning natural or merely human, living on the level of the soul’s instincts. Paul uses it for the natural man who receives not the things of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), and James for wisdom that is earthly and sensual (James 3:15). Far from being spiritual, they are “having not the Spirit.” The reference is to the Holy Spirit, whom Jude names in the next verse.

The Spirit’s work is to bind believers together in the unity of faith and love (Ephesians 4:3–6). Divisions, factions, and party spirit appear among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:19–21). The person who claims superior spirituality while fracturing the church shows by that very conduct that the Spirit is not leading. The test is the fruit, love, joy, and peace above all (Galatians 5:22–23), and this gift is never a badge of elite status.

wordNotes.explanation: This rare compound verb means to mark off or define by boundaries. Applied to people, it describes drawing lines that divide a community into rival groups. The same spirit troubled Corinth, where some said I am of Paul and others I am of Apollos.

The adjective derives from psychē, soul or life. In the New Testament it describes human nature apart from the Spirit, the natural life that cannot discern spiritual things. Paul uses it for the natural body that is sown in death, in contrast to the spiritual body raised at the resurrection.

verses.bibleText: But ye, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But ye, beloved.” For the second time Jude sets the faithful apart from the intruders, and now he tells them what to do. The instruction in verses 20–21 has one main command, “keep yourselves in the love of God,” surrounded by three supporting actions: building, praying, and looking. Contending for the faith (v. 3) turns out to be a constructive work.

“Building up yourselves on your most holy faith.” The pronoun is plural, and the building is shared. Believers strengthen one another, as stones fitted together into a temple for God (Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Peter 2:5). The intruders were tearing down; the church must build. The foundation is “your most holy faith,” the same body of truth once delivered to the saints (v. 3). It is holy because it comes from God and sets apart those who receive it, a sharp contrast with the ungodliness Jude has described. Steady growth in the apostolic teaching, the Scriptures studied, believed, and practiced, is the church’s first defense against error.

“Praying in the Holy Ghost.” The intruders were “having not the Spirit” (v. 19); the faithful pray in Him. To pray in the Spirit is to pray under His guidance and with His help, the Spirit who intercedes for us when we do not know what to ask (Romans 8:26–27; Ephesians 6:18). Prayer of this kind is no technique for spiritual experience. It is dependent communion with God, offered according to His will.

Across these two verses the Holy Spirit, the love of God, and the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ all appear. The whole Godhead is engaged in keeping the church faithful.

wordNotes.explanation: The compound verb means to build on top of a foundation already laid. Paul uses it for building upon Christ, the one foundation, and for being rooted and built up in Him. The present participle describes continuing construction, a lifelong work.

wordNotes.term: ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ προσευχόμενοι (en pneumati hagiō proseuchomenoi) — praying in the Holy Ghost
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes prayer prompted, shaped, and sustained by the Holy Spirit. It answers the charge that the intruders lacked the Spirit. Paul urges believers to pray always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit.

verses.bibleText: Keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Keep yourselves in the love of God.” This is the central command of Jude’s closing exhortation. The love in view is God’s love for His people, the love already resting on them as those “beloved in God the Father” (v. 1). They cannot earn it or create it. They are told to stay within it, to remain where that love is at work and to refuse every influence that would draw them away.

Jesus gave the same instruction in His farewell discourse: “continue ye in my love. If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love” (John 15:9–10). Obedience is the way believers remain in the place where divine love shelters them. The intruders had stepped outside it by turning grace into license. The faithful keep themselves there through the building and praying of verse 20, through fellowship, and through steady obedience to God’s word.

This command does not compete with God’s keeping. Jude began by calling them “preserved in Jesus Christ” (v. 1) and will end by praising Him “that is able to keep you from falling” (v. 24). God keeps His people, and His people keep themselves in His love. The two belong together. Peter says believers are kept by the power of God through faith (1 Peter 1:5), and faith is the human response through which divine power works.

They keep themselves “looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.” The verb describes eager expectation, the posture of a household waiting for its master’s return (Luke 12:36). Mercy is the gift they will receive when Christ appears, for even the most faithful will stand on that day by mercy alone (2 Timothy 1:18). That mercy leads “unto eternal life,” the life God will bestow in full when the dead are raised and the living are changed at Christ’s coming (1 Corinthians 15:51–54). Jude sets the church’s hope on that day. Its members live forward, toward their Lord.

wordNotes.explanation: The aorist imperative gives a decisive command. Jude uses the same verb family throughout: believers are kept for Christ (v. 1), angels who did not keep their place are kept for judgment (v. 6), and darkness is kept for the wanderers (v. 13). Those who keep themselves in God’s love escape the other kind of keeping.

The verb means to wait for with expectation and welcome. Luke uses it for Simeon waiting for the consolation of Israel and for Joseph of Arimathea waiting for the kingdom of God. It describes hopeful readiness for the Lord’s return.

verses.bibleText: And of some have compassion, making a difference:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jude’s concern now reaches beyond the faithful to those who have been affected by the intruders. The Greek text of verses 22–23 is uncertain at several points, and manuscripts vary between two and three groups. The KJV reads “of some have compassion, making a difference,” while many early witnesses read “have mercy on some who are doubting.” Either way, the sense is plain: different people need different kinds of help, and discernment must guide how mercy is shown.

Some are wavering, pulled between the apostolic faith and the new teaching. They need patient mercy. Jesus did not cast off the doubting. He stretched out His hand to Peter sinking in the waves (Matthew 14:31) and answered the father who cried, “help thou mine unbelief” (Mark 9:24). The church that contends for the faith must also be a church that gently holds on to those whose grip is slipping.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb can mean to distinguish, to dispute, or to waver in doubt. Jude used it in verse 9 for Michael’s dispute with the devil. Here it most likely describes those who doubt, as James uses it of the person who wavers like a wave of the sea.

verses.bibleText: And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire.” Some have moved further into danger and need urgent rescue. The verb “pulling” means to snatch or seize, the action of someone grabbing a person from a burning house. The image echoes Amos, who described Israel as “a firebrand plucked out of the burning” (Amos 4:11), and Zechariah, where the Lord says of Joshua the high priest, “Is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” (Zechariah 3:2). The fire recalls the judgment Jude has described in verse 7. Those who follow the intruders are on the edge of it, and love will not stand by and watch.

The rescue must be done “with fear.” This includes reverence before God and a sober awareness of personal danger. Paul told those who restore a fallen brother to consider themselves, “lest thou also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1). A rescuer who underestimates the pull of sin may be dragged into the same fire.

The final phrase describes the attitude that protects the rescuer: “hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.” The garment is the tunic worn next to the skin, the clothing most easily soiled by contact with the body. In Zechariah’s vision Joshua stands in filthy garments until the Lord commands, “Take away the filthy garments from him,” and clothes him in clean raiment (Zechariah 3:3–5). Believers love the sinner and loathe everything that defiles. They reach toward the person while keeping their distance from the contamination.

This is the gospel in miniature. Christ snatches sinners from the fire, strips away the soiled clothing of their past, and robes them in His own righteousness. Those who have received that rescue become instruments of it for others.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to seize quickly or snatch away, often by force. It describes the wolf catching the sheep and the believers caught up to meet the Lord. Here it conveys the urgency of rescue from imminent danger.

wordNotes.term: τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐσπιλωμένον χιτῶνα (ton apo tēs sarkos espilōmenon chitōna) — the garment spotted by the flesh
wordNotes.explanation: The chitōn was the inner tunic, worn against the skin. The participle means stained or defiled, from the same word family as the “spots” of verse 12. The picture is of clothing contaminated by contact with sin, which believers must refuse to touch while helping the one who wears it.

verses.bibleText: Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After all the warnings, Jude ends with praise. “Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling.” The whole letter has been leading here. Intruders have slipped in, apostasy threatens, and judgment is certain; yet God is able. His power is the final answer to every danger Jude has described.

The word “keep” here means to guard, as a sentry guards a city or a shepherd his flock. “From falling” translates a word meaning “without stumbling,” used of a sure-footed horse that does not trip on rough ground. God can keep His people steady on the path, even when false teachers make it treacherous. Those who place themselves under His keeping need not fall into the sins that ruined Israel, the angels, and Sodom. By His grace believers can live in victory over sin (1 John 3:6; 2 Peter 1:10).

God’s keeping reaches its goal on the day of judgment. He is able “to present you faultless before the presence of his glory.” “Faultless” is the word for a sacrificial animal without blemish. Paul uses it for the church Christ presents to Himself without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27) and for believers presented holy and unblameable in His sight (Colossians 1:22). No one stands in that presence by personal merit. Those who have been clothed in Christ’s righteousness and transformed by His Spirit will stand unashamed where the ungodly cannot.

They will stand “with exceeding joy.” The word describes exultant gladness, joy that breaks into celebration. The joy belongs both to the redeemed and to God Himself, who rejoices over His people with singing (Zephaniah 3:17). Christ endured the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2), and part of that joy is this moment, when the people He purchased stand before the Father, kept to the end.

wordNotes.explanation: Formed from the verb for stumbling with a negative prefix, the word means free from stumbling. James uses the verb when he says that in many things we all stumble. Jude praises God as able to keep believers sure-footed.

The word describes an offering without blemish, fit to be presented to God. Peter applies it to Christ, the Lamb without blemish, and Paul to the believers God chose to be holy and without blame before Him in love.

verses.bibleText: To the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“To the only wise God our Saviour.” The earliest manuscripts read simply “to the only God,” stressing that He alone is God. Against intruders who denied “the only Lord” (v. 4), Jude confesses the one true God, the God of Israel’s great confession (Deuteronomy 6:4). He calls the Father “our Saviour,” a title Scripture gives to both the Father and the Son (Luke 1:47; 1 Timothy 1:1; Titus 2:13). The oldest text adds “through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Salvation comes from the Father through the Son, and praise returns to the Father through Him.

Jude ascribes four qualities to God. “Glory” is the radiance of His character. “Majesty” is His greatness and exaltation, a word Hebrews uses when it says Christ sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3). “Dominion” is His might, the strength by which He rules. “Power” is His authority, His right to govern all things. The intruders had despised dominion (v. 8); Jude gives all dominion to God.

The ancient manuscripts also include the phrase “before all time,” so that the full sweep reads before all time, now, and forever. God’s glory has no beginning and no end. The letter closes with “Amen,” Jude’s own affirmation and an invitation for every reader to add theirs. A letter that began with intruders and judgment ends in worship, and it leaves the church facing the right direction: toward the God who keeps His people now and will receive their praise through all the ages to come.

wordNotes.explanation: Joined to the confession of the one God, the title names His saving purpose. Paul’s doxologies praise the King eternal, immortal, invisible, in similar terms. When Scripture calls the Father Saviour, it shows that redemption begins in His love and is carried out through His Son.
The word denotes greatness or majesty and in the New Testament refers only to God. Hebrews uses it as a reverent name for God Himself, at whose right hand Christ sits enthroned.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How can a church guard the truth it has received without becoming harsh toward those who are wavering?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Because God keeps His people, they are to hold fast the apostolic faith, reject the abuse of grace, and reach out in mercy to those endangered by error.
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that the faith was delivered “once” to the saints, and how should that shape the way we weigh new teaching?
How do the examples of Israel, the angels, and Sodom show that privilege does not protect anyone who persists in rebellion?
What does Michael’s restraint toward the devil teach about speech in conflict?
How do building, praying, keeping, and looking (vv. 20–21) work together as a defense against error?
How should mercy and caution operate together when we try to help someone drawn into sin?
commonMisunderstandings: Contending for the faith calls for faithfulness and courage, which is a different thing from a quarrelsome spirit.
“Eternal fire” in verse 7 describes a destruction whose result lasts forever; Sodom is not still burning.
Jude’s citation of Enoch’s prophecy does not make the whole book of 1 Enoch part of Scripture.
Keeping ourselves in God’s love does not compete with God’s keeping power; the one depends on the other.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold the letter’s frame together: the warnings are severe, yet they are spoken to people who are loved, kept, and called, and they end in praise to the God who is able to keep.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Stand firmly on the faith Christ gave through His apostles, keep yourself where God’s love is at work, and trust the One who can present you faultless before His glory.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s grace saves sinners and makes them holy, and the same God who calls them is able to keep them until Christ returns in mercy.
flow: God’s grace offers a salvation shared by all who believe.
That grace never licenses sin; those who twist it face certain judgment.
Christ rescues sinners like brands plucked from the fire and clothes them in His righteousness.
Those He rescues keep themselves in God’s love and wait for His mercy at His coming.
God is able to keep them from falling and present them faultless with joy.
simpleIllustrations: A lifeguard who pulls a drowning swimmer from the water acts quickly yet carefully, so that both are not lost.
A ship that stays within the channel markers is safe; one that ignores them runs onto hidden reefs.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let Christ pull you from danger and place your whole life in the keeping of the God who is able to present you faultless?
cautions: Do not use Jude’s strong language as a license to label or scorn people; Jude’s own model is Michael’s restraint.
Do not present final judgment as unending conscious torment; Scripture describes the end of the wicked as complete destruction.
Do not suggest that assurance rests on human effort apart from God’s keeping grace.

reflectionQuestions: Have I grown careless with God’s grace, treating it as room for sin instead of power for holiness?
Do I measure the teaching I hear by the faith once delivered, or by what is popular and pleasing?
How does my speech in conflict compare with Michael’s refusal to pronounce a railing accusation?
Am I keeping myself in God’s love through prayer, Scripture, and fellowship, or drifting toward its edges?
Whom do I know who is wavering, and how can I show them mercy without being drawn into their danger?
